newsitem.title: INDIA: India to allow private investment in coal mining.
newsitem.headline: India to allow private investment in coal mining.

text.p: India on Tuesday announced a sweeping restructuring of its ailing coal industry, throwing open exploration to the private sector and saying it would allow foreigners to take stakes in mining firms.
Coal Minister Kanti Singh told reporters the government was also negotiating with the World Bank to obtain $1 billion worth of loans for the restructuring of the state-owned Coal India Ltd (CIL).
"We are discussing with the World Bank to provide $1 billion for restructuring of CIL," Singh said. She did not elaborate.
CIL is the monopoly coal producer in the country.
The Coal Ministry said it proposed to allow Indian companies to mine coal and lignite for captive consumption and sale.
It also said in a statement it had decided to deregulate the prices and distribution of a specific grade of non-coking coal used in the cement industry.
"In order to meet the demand and supply gap, mainly demand from steel and power, the government has decided to invite the private sector in the coal industry," Singh said.
Singh said that the government also proposed to allow foreign equity in coal and lignite mining companies.
"Foreign equity will be allowed in Indian companies," Singh said, but added that foreign firms would not be invited to take part in exploration.
Officials said the Indian cabinet earlier on Tuesday decided on steps to revive the coal sector after considering a report of a panel set up to report on a long-term integrated coal policy.
The committee has estimated the demand for coal by India's power sector would rise to 350 million tonnes in 2001/02 (April-March) and 500 million tonnes by 2006/07 from 215 million tonnes in 1996/97.
The coal demand for the steel sector is estimated at 63 million tonnes in 2001/02 and 80 million tonnes in 2006/07.
India produced 273 million tonnes of coal in 1995/96.

The committee said the power sector plans to increase coal-based electricity generation capacity by 30,512 megawatts during the ninth five-year plan period (1997-2002) and by another 30,000 megawatts during the tenth plan (2002-2007).
But it said domestic coal output from the state-owned companies in the 1997-2002 period had been forecast to increase only by 61 million tonnes.
It said this could sustain new generation capacity of barely 8,800 megawatts of electricity.
The committee said the gap between demand and domestic availability, currently estimated at 35 million tonnes, might go up substantially.

The government also said on Tuesday it had decided to move a bill in parliament to amend the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 to allow any Indian company to mine coal and lignite not only for captive consumption but also for sale.
The statement also said the government had decided to deregulate pricing and distribution of hard coke used in steel making and soft coke used as a cooking fuel.

The government also plans to amend a 1957 Mines and Minerals Act and frame rules to set up an independent body to step up coal and lignite exploration, and to allocate mining blocks on the basis of a competitive bidding process.
